blocks.content: The Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) takes a genuinely different approach from HPA, instead of adjusting how many replicas exist, it adjusts how much CPU and memory each individual Pod is actually given.

Where HPA changes the number of Pods, VPA changes the resource requests and limits (covered in the Namespaces & Resource Management module) of the Pods that already exist, recommending, or automatically applying, better-sized values based on observed real usage.

blocks.alt: A fundamentally different lever, resource sizing instead of replica count

blocks.content: 2. Horizontal vs Vertical, the Actual Meaning
blocks.text: 2. Horizontal vs Vertical, the Actual Meaning

blocks.content: This is exactly where the terminology comes from, "horizontal" scaling means more or fewer instances, "vertical" scaling means bigger or smaller instances, the exact same distinction that applies to scaling any kind of server, not just Kubernetes Pods.

blocks.alt: The literal meaning behind the horizontal/vertical naming, made concrete

blocks.content: This is why VPA is covered here as a concept rather than in full operational depth: applying new resource values to an existing container generally requires restarting the Pod, there is currently no way to resize a running container's resources in place without at least a brief disruption.

blocks.alt: A genuine, current limitation, not something to overlook when considering VPA

blocks.content: This is a genuinely important, non-obvious gotcha: running VPA and HPA together, targeting the exact same metric (both watching CPU, for instance), creates a real conflict, VPA resizing Pods changes the very metric HPA is trying to react to, the two can fight each other rather than cooperate.

blocks.alt: Two autoscalers, potentially undermining each other on the same underlying metric

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: VPA adjusts a Pod's resource requests and limits (vertical scaling) rather than replica count (horizontal scaling, HPA's domain).
It has a real, current limitation, applying new values typically requires a Pod restart, and combining it with HPA on the same metric creates a genuine conflict worth avoiding.
